title: Reading set notation, sets, power sets, products, functions
summary: Read and write set-builder notation without guessing; tell ϕ, {ϕ}, and λ apart; build a power set and a Cartesian product with the right brackets; say what total and partial functions are in Chen's words; see why δ : Q × Σ → Q is coming.
sourceNote: Lesson 1 (Aug 24) and Lesson 2 (Aug 26) slides, Assignment 1 solution key.

sections.heading: Why a course about computers starts with sets

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **The plan behind the preliminaries** CS 154 asks a strange question: *what can a machine compute at all?* To answer it, Chen replaces real computers with mathematical toys — automata — and every toy is defined as a handful of sets and one function between them. A DFA (Lesson 5) is literally (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F): a set of states, a set of symbols, a function, a state, and a subset. So Lessons 1–2 aren't a review; ==they're the parts list==. Everything below reappears as a piece of a machine.
blocks.slide: The whole course is built from sets

blocks.body: **How Chen grades — read this before anything else** From the syllabus: **'Only use the notations mentioned in the class. Different notation(s) considered as wrong answer(s).'** From the Assignment 1 key: −0.5 for any notation error, −1 for an answer that's wrong but makes sense, −1.5 for major mistakes. Definitions marked ♥ on the slides must be reproduced almost word for word: 'a function where all of its domain elements are defined' was accepted; 'all domains are defined' was marked wrong. This chapter tells you which sentences those are.

sections.heading: Reading { … | … } — the notation that was costing you points

frames.caption: Set-builder notation. It looks like a formula; it's actually a *recipe for listing elements*. Read it in three parts: the braces, the left side, the right side.

lines: the braces say: this is a SET
frames.caption: Curly braces always mean 'a set'. Whatever is inside is a description of which elements belong. (Round brackets would mean something else — an ordered tuple. Chen takes 0.5 off for mixing them up.)

lines: the LEFT side is the shape of each element
frames.caption: Left of the bar `|` is a **pattern**: what every element looks like. Here each element is '3 times n' for some n. The bar itself reads as **'such that'** or **'where'**.

lines: the RIGHT side says which n are allowed
frames.caption: Right of the bar is the **condition**: which values of the variable you're allowed to plug into the pattern. Here n runs from 0 to 6. (Chen's default: variables are natural numbers, and 0 counts as natural.)
Now run the recipe: plug in every allowed n and collect the results.

That's the set — written out in **roster** form. Same set, two spellings. Set-builder is just shorter when the list would be long or infinite: { 3n | n ≥ 0 } is every multiple of 3, forever, and you couldn't list that.
One more convention that costs points: in the condition, a **comma means 'and'**. x ≥ 1 *and* x ≤ 5. If you mean 'or', you must write 'or' (or ∨) explicitly.

blocks.body: { pattern | condition }. Read the bar as **'such that'**. The set contains every value the pattern produces for every variable value the condition allows. Comma in the condition = **and**. The other two ways to write a set: **roster** — {0, 3, 6, …} with '…' when the pattern is obvious — and a **Venn diagram**.

blocks.title: Writing B = {0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18} and X = {0, 3, 6, 9, …}
blocks.body:
Give both in set-builder form and say whether each is finite.

1. Find the pattern: every element is a multiple of 3. So the left side is 3n.
2. Find the range of n. For B, n goes 0 to 6: B = { 3n | 0 ≤ n ≤ 6 }. Finite, |B| = 7.
3. For X the '…' means it never stops: X = { 3n | n ≥ 0 }. Infinite.
4. You may write n ∈ ℕ in the condition, but Chen's default universal set for variables is the natural numbers, so it can be left out.
blocks.slide: Going the other way: English → set-builder

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** Set-builder is the one notation from this course you will type almost daily, wearing different punctuation. Python's `[3*n for n in range(7)]` is { 3n | 0 ≤ n ≤ 6 } read left to right; SQL's `SELECT * FROM requests WHERE status = 500` is { r | r.status = 500 }; a TypeScript `.filter(x => x >= 1 && x <= 5)` is the condition side of the bar, comma-as-and included. ==Pattern on the left, condition on the right== is the shape of every query language ever shipped — learn to read it here and list comprehensions stop being magic.

blocks.prompt: List the elements of { 2n + 1 | 0 ≤ n ≤ 3 }, and write {1, 4, 9, 16, …} in set-builder.

blocks.body: a collection of objects (its elements or members). Order does not matter and repeats don't count: {3, 4, 1, 3, 2} = {1, 2, 3, 4}. A **list** is the ordered version — a different concept.
the number of elements. |{1, 3, 1, 6, 5}| = 4 (the repeated 1 counts once).
a set whose size is a natural number. (0 is natural here, so ϕ is finite.) ♥ **Infinite set**: a set whose size cannot be expressed by a natural number, e.g. ℕ = {0, 1, 2, …}.
the set of all possible elements under consideration — the rectangle in a Venn diagram.
Ā = { x | x ∈ U, x ∉ A }: everything in U that's not in A. You cannot take a complement without knowing U.

**ϕ versus {ϕ} — a favorite trick question** ϕ is the empty set: nothing inside, |ϕ| = 0. {ϕ} is a set with **one** element, and that element happens to be the empty set: |{ϕ}| = 1. A box with nothing in it versus a box containing an empty box. In Lesson 3 a third thing joins them — λ, the empty *string* — and telling all three apart is worth points on every quiz.
sets share at least one element; **disjoint** sets share none.
A ⊆ B: every element of A is also in B. **Proper subset** A ⊂ B: A ⊆ B *and* A ≠ B. If A = {2, 5, 3} and B = {3, 5, 2}, then A ⊆ B is right and A ⊂ B is **wrong** — they're equal.
A = B exactly when A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.

blocks.md: Two different kinds of claims need two different symbols, and mixing them is a classic deduction. **∈ relates an element to a set**: x ∈ A says the *thing* x is one of A's members; x ∉ A says it isn't. **⊆ relates two sets** (previous definition): every member of the left one is in the right one. So 1 ∈ {1, 2} is true, but !!{1} ∈ {1, 2} is false!! — the elements are 1 and 2, and the *set* {1} is neither of them. The true statement there is {1} ⊆ {1, 2}. Before writing either symbol, ask: is the thing on my left an element or a set?

blocks.body: the complement of A ∩ B is Ā ∪ B̄; the complement of A ∪ B is Ā ∩ B̄. (Flip the operation, complement each part.)

blocks.md:
Why drill these now? In two weeks a *language* will be defined as a set of strings — so every way of combining sets becomes a way of combining languages, for free. The operations, each written in the set-builder you just learned:
- **Union** A ∪ B = { x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B } (in either). **Intersection** A ∩ B = { x | x ∈ A, x ∈ B } (in both — note the comma meaning *and*). **Difference** A − B = { x | x ∈ A, x ∉ B } (in A but not B). **Complement** Ā = U − A.
- Union and intersection are commutative, associative, distributive. !!Difference is none of those!! — A − B ≠ B − A, the sanity check worth two seconds on every quiz.
- Identity A ∪ ϕ = A, A ∩ U = A. Domination A ∪ U = U, A ∩ ϕ = ϕ. Idempotent A ∪ A = A. Complement A ∪ Ā = U, A ∩ Ā = ϕ. Double complement gives A back.
blocks.slide: Operations and the identities he lists

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** Set algebra is boolean logic wearing braces, and it escapes the classroom constantly. Every time you refactor `!(isAdmin && isActive)` into `!isAdmin || !isActive`, that's ==De Morgan== — the same law, the same flip. SQL ships UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT as keywords; `grep -v` is complement; a permission system intersects the roles you have with the roles a route requires. And ϕ-versus-{ϕ} is the difference between `[]` and `[[]]` in code, or between an API returning 'no results' and returning one empty result — a gap real bugs live in.

blocks.prompt: Is {ϕ} the empty set? Is ϕ ⊆ {1, 2}? Is {1, 2} ⊂ {1, 2}?
blocks.answer: No — it has one element. Yes — the empty set is a subset of everything. No — proper subset requires the sets to differ; {1, 2} ⊆ {1, 2} is the correct statement.

sections.heading: Power set: the set of all subsets

frames.caption: The **power set** of A, written 2ᴬ, is the set of *all subsets* of A. Let's list them for A = {a, b} by asking, for each element, 'in or out?'
Both out: the empty set ϕ. Yes, ϕ is a subset of every set — it's always in the power set.
Both in: A itself. Every set is a subset of itself.

Written out with **outer braces** (it's a set) and **inner braces** (each element is itself a set). Two elements, each in-or-out, gives 2 × 2 = 4 subsets. In general |2ᴬ| = 2^|A| — which is exactly why it's called 2ᴬ.

blocks.body: 2ᴬ = { X | X ⊆ A }, the set of all subsets of A. |2ᴬ| = 2^|A|. Always includes ϕ and A itself.

**Assignment 1 Q12 — the deductions** Power set of {c, d} must be written **{ϕ, {c}, {d}, {c, d}}∗*: outer braces *and* inner braces. Marked down: round brackets instead of braces; writing {ϕ} when you mean the empty set as an element (that's a set containing the empty set, a different thing). Spelling out 'phi' is accepted.

blocks.md: In Lesson 8, a nondeterministic automaton's transition function will map to a *set of states* rather than a single state. Its range is ==2^Q — the power set of the state set==. When Chen asks 'what is the range of δ for an NFA', this is the answer, and this is where he taught it.

**Where you'll meet this after the exam** |2ᴬ| = 2^|A| is the formula behind every combinatorial explosion you'll ever be warned about. n boolean feature flags give 2ⁿ possible configurations — the power set of the flag set — which is why nobody tests every combination. An n-bit integer enumerates exactly the subsets of an n-element set, one bit per 'in or out?' answer, which is why bitmask tricks work at all: subset ↔ number. And in three weeks the NFA's δ lands in 2^Q — ##learn power sets now and Lesson 8 costs you nothing##.

blocks.prompt: Write 2ᴬ for A = {1, 2, 3}. How many elements should it have before you start?

sections.heading: Cartesian product: all the ordered pairs

blocks.label: why
blocks.md: **Where pairs come from** A DFA's brain makes a decision from two things at once: *which state am I in* and *which symbol did I just read*. A decision that depends on two inputs is a function of the **pair** (state, symbol). The Cartesian product is how you build ==the set of all such pairs== — so the transition function has a domain to be defined on.

frames.caption: Assignment 1 Q16. Two sets, and a product of them. First simplify the thing in parentheses.
Union: everything in either set. Three elements now. (λ is the empty string — a symbol-like thing you'll meet properly in Lesson 3. Here it's just a third element.)

lines: = every (element of Q, element of the other) pair
first from Q, second from {x, y, λ}
frames.caption: **Cartesian product** A × B: the set of all ordered pairs (a, b) with a from A and b from B. Order matters inside the pair — (m, x) and (x, m) are different, and only the first belongs here.
Take m, pair it with each of x, y, λ. Three pairs.
Take n, same thing. Three more.

The answer: outer **braces** (a set), each element in **parentheses** (an ordered pair). |A × B| = |A| · |B| — always check your count. Chen's key: writing 'lambda' in words is fine; wrong brackets are −0.5.

blocks.body: { (a, b) | a ∈ A, b ∈ B }: every ordered pair with first part from A and second from B. |A × B| = |A|·|B|. A × ϕ = ϕ. **Not commutative** — A × B ≠ B × A unless A = B or one is empty, because pairs are ordered. Extends to more sets: Q × Σ × Γ is a set of 3-tuples.

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** Pairing every element of one set with every element of another is a pattern you'll recognize everywhere once it has a name. SQL's CROSS JOIN is literally A × B (and an accidental one is the classic query that returns a million rows). A tuple type like `[string, number]` is an element of String × Number — type theorists call these ==product types== for exactly this reason. Nested loops `for a in A: for b in B:` enumerate a Cartesian product. And next week a DFA's transition function takes its input from Q × Σ — every (state, symbol) pair — which is why this grid, rows as states and columns as symbols, is about to become the transition table.

blocks.prompt: A = {1, 2}, B = {p}. Write A × B and B × A. Are they equal?

blocks.md: f : D → R takes each element of the **domain** D to **one** element of the **range** R. ==One input, at most one output== — that's the rule. Several inputs may share an output (f(1) = f(2) = 5 is fine); one input may not have two outputs. You can write a function as algebra (f(x) = 2x), as arrows in a diagram, or as a set of ordered pairs (input, output) — and that set of pairs is a subset of D × R. That's the link to the Cartesian product.
blocks.slide: A function is a rule with one answer

blocks.md: **♥ Total and partial — the exact wording** **Total function**: a function where **all elements of its domain are defined**. **Partial function**: at least one domain element is undefined (has no output). The key accepted 'a function that all of its domain elements are defined' and rejected 'all domains are defined', 'the function is defined', 'all elements are defined'. !!The words *domain elements* must be there.!!

Middle: partial — element 2 fires no arrow, so it's undefined. Right: not a function at all — element 1 fires two. Hover each panel for what makes it legal or illegal.

blocks.title: Spotting a non-function
blocks.body:
Q = {q₀, q₁}, Γ = {a, b}, δ : Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R}. Can δ = { ((q₀,a), (q₀,a,L)), ((q₀,a), (q₀,b,L)) } be a function?

1. Read the pairs as (input, output). Both pairs have the same input, (q₀, a).
2. The outputs differ: (q₀, a, L) versus (q₀, b, L).
3. One input with two outputs breaks the rule. **Not a function.**
4. (That δ shape — state and symbol in, state and symbol and a direction out — is a Turing machine's. He's planting it in week 2.)
blocks.answer: No: the same domain element maps to two range elements.
blocks.slide: Assignment 1: can this δ be a function?

blocks.md: Read it aloud: 'delta is a function from Q cross Sigma to Q.' Domain: the set of (state, symbol) pairs — the Cartesian product from the previous section. Range: the set of states. In words: *given a state and a symbol, δ tells you the next state.* That is the entire brain of a DFA, and if δ is **total** (every pair has an answer), the machine always knows what to do. Lesson 5 will draw it as arrows; this is what the arrows mean.
blocks.slide: The one function that matters: δ : Q × Σ → Q

blocks.md: **Where you'll meet this after the exam** 'One input, exactly one output' is the contract of every lookup you'll ever write: a hash map is a function stored as data — `Map<K, V>` gives one value per key, by construction. A *partial* function is any function that can throw or come back empty — `parseInt` on 'hello', a cache miss — and half of defensive programming is handling the domain elements someone left undefined. TypeScript's exhaustive `switch` with a `never` check is a ==totality check the compiler runs for you==: the same 'is every domain element defined?' question Chen asks about δ, and the question that decides whether a state machine can ever be surprised by its input.

blocks.prompt: D = {1, 2, 3}, R = {a, b}. f = {(1, a), (3, b)}. Is f a function? Total or partial?
blocks.answer: It's a function (no input has two outputs). Partial — 2 is a domain element with no output.

blocks.body: a walk can revisit vertices, so drawn on the graph it tangles over itself. The projection untangles it: write the walk out as a straight line — v₁ → v₃ → v₁ → v₃ → v₂ — repeats and all. Now its length (the number of edges, 4 here) is countable at a glance. This is exactly the trace format for running a DFA on a string.

blocks.md:
- A **graph** is a non-empty finite set of **vertices** V and a finite set of **edges** E. This course uses **directed** graphs only: an edge is an ordered pair (from, to) — an arrow.
- A **walk** is a sequence of edges where each edge ends where the next one begins. 'We cannot jump.' Its **length** is the number of edges.

A DFA's control unit is drawn as a directed graph: vertices are states, edges are transitions labelled with symbols. ==Running the machine on a string is *taking a walk*== — one edge per symbol read — and the one-dimensional projection of that walk is the machine's trace. When Lesson 5 says 'the machine follows the transition', it means 'takes the next edge in the walk'.

**Where you'll meet this after the exam** Directed graphs are the most reused picture in computing: package dependency trees (an `npm` cycle is a walk that comes home), git's commit graph, routing tables, build pipelines. The 'we cannot jump' rule is exactly how you debug a redirect chain — each hop must start where the last one ended, and the chain's length is its projection. And next lesson makes the connection literal: a protocol like TCP's connection setup is published *as* a directed graph of states, and a handshake is nothing but a three-edge walk through it.

**Lessons 1–2 in one breath.** Sets hold the pieces (states Q, symbols Σ). The Cartesian product Q × Σ makes (state, symbol) pairs. A total function δ : Q × Σ → Q picks the next state for each pair. Drawn as a directed graph, running the machine is a walk. The power set 2^Q shows up when a machine is allowed several next states at once (NFA).

exercises.title: Read three set-builders
exercises.prompt: List the elements (roster form) of: (a) { 2n | 1 ≤ n ≤ 4 }, (b) { x | x ∈ ℕ, x < 3 }, (c) { n² | n ∈ ℕ, n² < 30 }. Say which are finite.
hints: Left of the bar is the shape of each element; right of the bar is which variable values are allowed. Plug every allowed value into the shape.
For (b), people forget that 0 is a natural number in this class. For (c), don't stop at n = 4 — check n = 5: 25 < 30, so it's in. n = 6 gives 36, out.
Write the answer with braces and commas. If it's infinite you'd need '…'; none of these are.
solution: (b) natural numbers below 3, with 0 included → {0, 1, 2}. Finite, size 3.
exercises.why: Set-builder is the notation of every specification you'll read as an engineer — 'the set of requests r such that r.status = 500' is exactly { r | r.status = 500 }. SQL's WHERE clause, list comprehensions in Python, and type predicates are all this notation with different punctuation.

exercises.title: Which statements are true?
exercises.prompt: Decide true or false, and fix each false one with a single change: (a) |{ϕ}| = 0. (b) ϕ ⊆ {a, b}. (c) {a, b} ⊂ {a, b}. (d) ϕ ∈ {ϕ}. (e) {1, 2} = {2, 1, 1}.
hints: For each, ask what kind of thing is on each side: an element? a set? a set containing a set? The symbols ∈ and ⊆ need different kinds of things on their left.
The most-missed one is (a): {ϕ} is a box containing an empty box — one thing inside. And (c): ⊂ (proper) demands the sets be different.
For (e): sets ignore order and repeats. Read both sides as 'which distinct things are in here'.
solution: (b) True: the empty set is a subset of every set.
(c) False: a set is not a proper subset of itself. Fix: {a, b} ⊆ {a, b}.
(d) True: ϕ is the one element of {ϕ}.
(e) True: both are the set containing exactly 1 and 2.
exercises.why: The difference between 'an empty collection' and 'a collection containing an empty collection' is the difference between `[]` and `[[]]` in code — and between 'no result' and 'a result that is empty' in an API. Bugs live in that gap.

exercises.title: Product, then function
exercises.prompt: Q = {p, q}, Σ = {0, 1}. (a) Write Q × Σ in roster form and give its size. (b) Define a *total* function δ : Q × Σ → Q of your choice as a set of ordered pairs. (c) Change one pair so δ becomes partial, and one different change so it stops being a function at all.
hints: (a) is mechanical: every (state, symbol) pair, in parentheses, inside one set of braces. Count = |Q| · |Σ|.

Chen's deductions here are all brackets: tuples in ( ), the set in { }. And a function 'as ordered pairs' means pairs of the form (input, output) — here ((p, 0), q), a pair whose first part is itself a pair.
Total means every one of the four inputs has an output. Partial: delete one. Not a function: give one input two different outputs.
solution: (b) e.g. δ = {((p, 0), p), ((p, 1), q), ((q, 0), q), ((q, 1), p)} — all four inputs defined, one output each. Total.
(c) Partial: remove ((q, 1), p) — input (q, 1) now has no output. Not a function: add ((p, 0), q) alongside ((p, 0), p) — one input, two outputs.
exercises.why: This δ is literally the transition table of a state machine — the thing that runs a vending machine, a TCP connection, or a UI's screen flow. 'Total' means the machine can never be surprised by an input; a partial δ is the bug where the app has no idea what to do when you press a button at the wrong time.
